prompt: In the FTP capture, how did the password travel?

choices.text: Hashed with MD5, as FTP servers expect
choices.why: FTP sends no hash.

choices.text: As typed, after PASS
choices.why: Right: readable by anybody on the path.

choices.text: Encrypted with the server's certificate
choices.why: This FTP server has no TLS at all.

choices.text: Encoded in Base64 inside the USER command
choices.why: It was plain text in its own command.

prompt: Why did `curl --ssl-reqd` stop before sending USER and PASS?

choices.text: Because the password was wrong
choices.why: It never got as far as the password.

choices.text: Because port 2121 is reserved for FTPS
choices.why: Ports do not decide this.

choices.text: TLS was required but unavailable
choices.why: Right: a client that only preferred TLS would have sent the password.

choices.text: Because curl does not support FTP
choices.why: The first command used FTP successfully.

prompt: Match each plain protocol to its encrypted replacement.
On which port does LDAPS listen by default?
Why did Ana compare the fingerprint from `ssh-keyscan` with the one the administrator published, before saving the key?
hint: SSH has no CA by default.

choices.text: To make the connection faster next time
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Because sftp refuses ed25519 keys otherwise
choices.why: It accepts them.

choices.text: To encrypt the fingerprint before storing it
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted in known_hosts.

choices.text: To be sure the key is the server's
choices.why: Right: the first connection is when an impostor could slip in.

prompt: What did the SSH connection use as its key exchange?
hint: The first line of the verbose output.

choices.text: A post-quantum hybrid
choices.why: Right: sntrup761x25519-sha512.

choices.text: RSA key transport with the host key
choices.why: SSH never transports keys that way.

choices.text: ChaCha20-Poly1305
choices.why: That is the cipher, chosen after the exchange.

choices.text: Ana's Ed25519 key
choices.why: That authenticated Ana; it did not agree the key.

prompt: A team runs 300 servers and users keep answering yes to new host keys without checking. Which change removes the question rather than asking people to be careful?

choices.text: Disable StrictHostKeyChecking everywhere
choices.why: That accepts every key without asking, which is worse.

choices.text: SSH certificates signed by an internal CA
choices.why: Right: clients trust the CA, not each key.

choices.text: Use RSA host keys instead of Ed25519
choices.why: The algorithm is not the problem.

choices.text: Rotate all host keys every month
choices.why: That would make people answer yes more often.

prompt: SFTP runs inside an ___ connection, while FTPS is FTP wrapped in TLS.

hint: SSL is the old name of what?

choices.text: A certificate that only works with SSL 3.0
choices.why: SSL 3.0 is prohibited and unused.

choices.text: A weaker kind of certificate than a TLS one
choices.why: They are the same thing.

choices.text: A TLS certificate under its old name
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A certificate signed by Netscape
choices.why: Netscape designed SSL; it signs nothing now.

prompt: Why can STARTTLS be stripped while implicit TLS cannot?

choices.text: STARTTLS uses an older version of TLS
choices.why: It negotiated TLS 1.3 in the lab.

choices.text: Its upgrade request travels in clear text first
choices.why: Right: an attacker is able to remove the offer.

choices.text: Implicit TLS uses longer keys
choices.why: Key length is unrelated.

choices.text: STARTTLS skips certificate verification
choices.why: The lab's STARTTLS verified the certificate.

prompt: Which of these defend against STARTTLS stripping? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A client option that refuses to continue without TLS
choices.why: Yes: -ZZ, --ssl-reqd.

choices.text: MTA-STS for mail between domains
choices.why: Yes: it publishes that TLS is required.

choices.text: Using implicit TLS where available
choices.why: Yes: nothing to strip.

choices.text: Listing STARTTLS first among the server's capabilities
choices.why: The attacker removes it wherever it is listed.

prompt: The directory answered `confidentiality required` to a plain bind. What did that refusal protect?

choices.text: That password, which never left the client

choices.text: The directory's TLS certificate
choices.why: The certificate was not involved.

choices.text: Clients that send it fail loudly

choices.text: Nothing: the bind succeeded anyway
choices.why: It did not succeed.

prompt: An LDAPS client prints `Can't contact LDAP server`, but the server is running. What should be checked first?

choices.text: The firewall on port 389
choices.why: LDAPS uses 636, and the server was reachable.

choices.text: Whether TLS_REQCERT is set to never
choices.why: Setting it to never would hide the problem, not solve it.

choices.text: The admin password
choices.why: A wrong password gives a different error.

choices.text: Trust in Vereda's CA on that machine
choices.why: Right: -d 1 shows the TLS error.

choices.text: Compression of the LDAP traffic
choices.why: It has nothing to do with compression.

choices.text: StartTLS, required
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A connection to port 636 instead of 389
choices.why: That would be ldaps://.

choices.text: Anonymous binding
choices.why: The bind still used the admin name.
